# Markup vs. Margin: What is the Difference?


- by[Francesca Nicasio](https://www.lightspeedhq.com/blog/author/francesca-nicasio/)
- 2026-11-17

Markup is the percentage you add to your wholesale cost to set a retail price, while profit margin is the percentage of that final selling price you actually keep as profit. Mixing up these two metrics is one of the fastest ways to accidentally underprice your inventory and quietly erode your bottom line.


Whether you are pricing a new apparel line or calculating food costs for a second location, getting the math right dictates your financial health. We will break down the exact formulas for both metrics, show you how to convert between them and explain when to use each to protect your revenue.

## **What are markup and margin?**


Markup is the percentage added to the cost of a product to determine its selling price, while margin is the percentage of the selling price that is profit. Both metrics represent the exact same dollar amount of profit, but using different denominators changes the percentages drastically. Understanding the difference between profit margin and markup helps you set accurate prices and evaluate your business’s financial health.


You might be wondering why this distinction matters. Mixing up markup and margin often leads to pricing errors, especially when scaling a retail or restaurant business across multiple locations. Let’s break down exactly what each term means.


### **What is markup?**


Markup focuses entirely on the cost of the goods you sell. It answers a simple question: how much do you add to the wholesale price you paid?


Retailers often use markup when[setting initial prices](https://www.lightspeedhq.com/blog/how-to-price-product/) to ensure they cover wholesale costs and generate a profit. For example, if you buy a shirt for $10 and sell it for $20, you added a 100% markup.


This metric is incredibly useful for inventory managers. When a new shipment arrives, applying a standard markup percentage helps you quickly generate retail prices across hundreds of items.


### **What is profit margin?**


Profit margin looks at the revenue you bring in from a sale. It tells you how much of every dollar you earn is actually kept as profit after paying for the cost of goods sold.


The[cost of goods sold](https://www.lightspeedhq.com/blog/what-is-cogs/) , often called COGS, includes the direct costs of producing or buying the items you sell. Margin is typically used to evaluate overall financial performance rather than to set individual item prices.


If you want to know if your business is truly profitable, you look at your margins. A high markup does not always guarantee a high margin, which is a common pitfall for growing businesses.


## **Key differences between markup and margin**


While both metrics measure profitability, they serve entirely different purposes in your day-to-day operations. Confusing markup and margin can lead to inaccurate financial forecasting.


You might be thinking that as long as you make a profit, the specific metric does not matter. However, as your business grows and evolves, tracking the right numbers becomes critical. Let’s look at how they differ in practice.


### **Basis of calculation**


The fundamental difference between markup and margin lies in the denominator used for the calculation. Markup is calculated based on your cost, whereas margin is calculated based on your total revenue.


Because markup uses cost as the denominator, it will always be a higher percentage than margin. Margin uses revenue as the denominator, which is always a larger number than cost.


### **Impact on pricing strategy**


You will typically use markup when deciding how to price a new product on your shelves. It gives you a straightforward multiplier to apply to your[wholesale costs](https://www.lightspeedhq.com/blog/wholesale-vs-retail/) .


[Pricing strategies](https://www.lightspeedhq.com/blog/9-retail-pricing-strategies-that-get-customers-to-buy/) rely heavily on markup to maintain consistency. If you know your target markup, you can quickly price new inventory without overthinking it. For instance, a restaurant might apply a standard 300% markup to all ingredients to ensure[food costs](https://www.lightspeedhq.com/blog/how-to-calculate-restaurant-food-costs/) stay manageable.


### **Effect on profitability**


Margin helps you measure how much money you actually made after a sale is complete. At the end of the month, you look at your profit margins to see if you generated enough revenue to cover fixed costs.


Fixed costs include expenses like rent, payroll and marketing. Margin tells you if your[pricing strategy](https://www.lightspeedhq.com/blog/restaurant-menu-pricing/) is actually working to cover these overhead expenses. Profitability is the ultimate measure of your business’s success, and margin gives you a clear picture of how much cash is available to reinvest.


### **Common business use cases**


Different departments often rely on different metrics to do their jobs. Here is how different roles use these numbers:


- **Inventory managers:** Buyers use markup to negotiate better wholesale rates and[set initial retail prices](https://www.lightspeedhq.com/blog/how-to-price-wholesale-inventory/) .
- **Finance teams:** Accountants use margin to forecast revenue,[manage cash flow](https://www.lightspeedhq.com/blog/cash-flow-management/) and prepare tax documents.
- **Business owners:** Entrepreneurs look at margin to determine if they can afford to open a new location or hire more staff.

## **Markup vs margin formula**


Both metrics rely on the same basic inputs of cost and selling price. However, the formulas yield very different percentages.


Understanding the math behind these metrics is essential for any business owner. Let’s look at the exact formulas you use to calculate them.


### **Markup formula**


The markup formula measures how much the selling price exceeds the cost, expressed as a percentage of that cost.


To find the markup percentage, use this equation: ((Selling price – Cost) / Cost) x 100.


In this equation, the cost is your COGS and the selling price is what the customer pays. The markup formula is relatively simple because you take your gross profit and divide it by your cost.


### **Profit margin formula**


The margin formula measures the percentage of revenue you retain as profit.


To find the margin percentage, use this equation: ((Selling price – Cost) / Selling price) x 100.


Notice how the denominator changes to the selling price. This shift is exactly why your margin will always be a lower percentage than your markup. The margin formula is equally simple but uses a different base, dividing your gross profit by your total revenue.


## **How to calculate markup and margin (with example)**


Let’s walk through how to calculate markup and margin using a real-world scenario. We will use a simple retail product to see how the math plays out.


To truly grasp these concepts, it helps to see them in action. Let’s walk through a practical example.


### **How to calculate markup?**


Calculating markup is a straightforward process that starts with knowing exactly what you paid for an item. Calculating markup requires you to know your exact costs, including the wholesale price, shipping fees and any other direct expenses.


#### **Markup calculation steps**


Follow these steps to find your markup percentage:


- **Step 1:** Determine the exact cost of goods sold for the item.
- **Step 2:** Subtract the cost from your final selling price to find your gross profit.
- **Step 3:** Divide that gross profit by the original cost.
- **Step 4:** Multiply the result by 100 to convert the decimal into a percentage.


#### **Example of markup calculation**


Imagine you run a boutique and buy a jacket from a wholesaler for $50. You decide to sell that jacket for $100.


Your profit is $50, which is the $100 selling price minus the $50 cost. To find the markup, divide the $50 profit by the $50 cost, which equals 1.


Multiply by 100, and you have a 100% markup.


### **How to calculate profit margin?**


Now, let’s look at the exact same jacket from a profitability perspective. Calculating margin requires you to know your final selling price, which is the amount the customer actually pays at the register.


#### **Margin calculation steps**


The process is similar, but the final division changes:


- **Step 1:** Identify the final selling price of the item.
- **Step 2:** Subtract the cost from the selling price to determine your gross profit.
- **Step 3:** Divide the gross profit by the selling price.
- **Step 4:** Multiply the decimal by 100 to convert it to a percentage.


#### **Example of margin calculation**


Using the same jacket, your cost is $50 and your selling price is $100. Your gross profit remains $50.


This time, divide the $50 profit by the $100 selling price, which gives you 0.5. Multiply by 100, and you get a 50% profit margin.


Even though the dollar amount of profit is identical, the 100% markup only yields a 50% margin.


## **Markup vs margin: Conversion rules**


Because markup and margin are mathematically linked, you can easily convert one into the other. This is incredibly helpful when a supplier quotes a markup but you want to know your actual profit margin.


Converting between these two metrics is a common task in retail and hospitality. You might be thinking that doing this math in your head is difficult, but the conversion formulas are simple to use.


### **Converting markup to margin**


To convert a markup percentage into a margin percentage, use this simple formula: Margin = Markup / (1 + Markup).


For example, if you have a 50% markup, you express it as 0.50 and divide 0.50 by 1.50. This gives you 0.333, meaning a 50% markup equals a 33.3% margin.


This conversion is vital when you are trying to forecast your monthly revenue based on supplier pricing.


### **Converting margin to markup**


If you have a target profit margin in mind and want to know how much to mark up your products, the formula reverses: Markup = Margin / (1 – Margin).


If your goal is a 20% margin, you express it as 0.20 and divide 0.20 by 0.80. This equals 0.25, meaning you apply a 25% markup to your wholesale cost to hit your target.


This is the exact math you use when building a pricing strategy from scratch.

## **When to use markup vs margin in pricing**


Knowing the math is great, but applying it correctly is what actually grows your business. Let’s explore when to use each metric.


Applying these metrics correctly is crucial for long-term success. Choosing the right metric depends entirely on the task at hand.


### **When businesses use markup**


Markup is your go-to tool for cost-based pricing. When a new shipment of inventory arrives, applying a standard markup percentage helps you quickly generate retail prices across hundreds of items.


It is a fast, scalable way to ensure your baseline costs are covered before items hit the sales floor. For example, a hardware store might apply a flat 40% markup to all small hand tools to streamline their pricing process.


### **When businesses use margin**


Margin is used when you are analyzing the overall health of your business. At the end of the month, you look at your profit margins to see if you generated enough revenue to cover fixed costs.


Margin tells you if your pricing strategy is actually working. If your margins are too low, you will struggle to pay rent or expand to a second location. Investors and bank lenders will also look exclusively at your margins when evaluating your business for a loan.


### **Why confusing the two can affect profitability**


Mixing up markup and margin can lead to[disastrous financial results](https://www.lightspeedhq.com/blog/money-mistakes-small-businesses-make-during-the-first-year/) . If your accountant says you require a 40% margin to stay profitable, and you mistakenly apply a 40% markup to your products, your actual margin will only be 28.5%.


The biggest danger is assuming that a 50% markup equals a 50% margin. As we have seen, a 50% markup actually results in a 33.3% margin.


Across a high volume of sales or multiple store locations, that 11.5% discrepancy can wipe out your entire bottom line. This is why ambitious retailers rely on advanced ecommerce and POS platforms to keep their pricing and reporting perfectly aligned.

## **FAQs about markup vs margin**


### **What is a good margin for a small business?**


A good profit margin varies heavily by industry, but a 10% net margin is generally considered average for a small business. Retailers often aim for[retail profit margins](https://www.lightspeedhq.com/blog/retail-profit-margins/) between 40% and 50%, while restaurants typically operate on[much tighter margins](https://www.lightspeedhq.com/blog/complete-guide-to-restaurant-profit-margins/) . Benchmark against competitors in your specific sector to gauge your success.


### **What are common mistakes with markup and margin?**


The most common mistake is using the terms interchangeably, which leads to setting prices too low to cover operating expenses. Another frequent error is calculating margin based on the wholesale cost instead of the final selling price, which can leave you unable to cover[operating expenses](https://www.lightspeedhq.com/blog/what-are-operating-expenses/) .


### **Is a 30% profit margin too high?**


A 30% profit margin is not inherently too high, as many retail and ecommerce businesses require margins in this range to remain profitable. However, if a 30% margin pushes your retail price far above market value, you risk losing customers to competitors.


### **Can a business use both markup and margin?**


Yes, successful businesses use both metrics simultaneously for different purposes. Buyers use markup to set initial retail prices, while finance teams use margin to evaluate the overall profitability of the company.


### **Why do retailers use markup instead of margin?**


Retailers use markup for pricing because it provides a simple, repeatable formula to apply to wholesale costs as new inventory arrives. It is much faster to multiply a cost by a set markup percentage than to calculate the target margin for every individual item.
